content: Tafenoquine can increase the levels or effects of varenicline due to its inhibition of organic cation transporter-2 (OCT2) and multidrug and toxin extrusion (MATE) transporters in vitro. Co-administration with OCT2 or MATE substrates should be avoided. If co-administration is unavoidable, monitor for toxicities related to the substrate and consider dosage adjustments based on the labeling of the co-administered drug. Patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency are at risk of hemolytic anemia when prescribed tafenoquine. G6PD testing must be performed prior to prescribing the drug. Patients should be advised to seek medical attention if signs of hemolysis occur. Use of tafenoquine during pregnancy or breastfeeding may cause hemolytic anemia in a G6PD-deficient fetus or infant, respectively. Asymptomatic elevations in methemoglobin have been observed; appropriate therapy should be initiated if signs or symptoms of methemoglobinemia occur. Individuals with NADH-dependent methemoglobin reductase deficiency should be carefully monitored. Psychiatric adverse reactions, such as anxiety, abnormal dreams, and insomnia, have been reported in clinical trials. The benefits of treatment must be weighed against the potential risks of psychiatric adverse reactions, particularly in patients with a history of psychiatric illness. Due to the long half-life of tafenoquine (~15 days for Krintafel or ~17 days for Arakoda), the onset and/or duration of psychiatric adverse reactions may be delayed. Serious hypersensitivity reactions, including angioedema and urticaria, have been reported. If such reactions occur, appropriate therapy should be initiated, and tafenoquine should not be re-administered. The long half-life of the drug may result in delayed onset and/or duration of hypersensitivity symptoms. Available data in pregnant women are insufficient to establish a drug-associated risk of major birth defects, miscarriage, or adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. However, tafenoquine use during pregnancy is not recommended due to the potential risk of hemolytic anemia in a G6PD-deficient fetus. Similarly, breastfeeding women should be advised of the potential risk of hemolytic anemia in a G6PD-deficient infant. The G6PD status of the infant should be checked before breastfeeding begins. If the infant is G6PD-deficient, breastfeeding should be avoided for three months after the maternal dose. There is no data on the presence of tafenoquine in human milk, its effects on the breastfed infant, or its effects on milk production. In infants with normal G6PD levels, the developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding should be considered alongside the mother’s clinical need for the drug and any potential effects on the infant. Tafenoquine is an antiplasmodial 8-aminoquinoline derivative with activity against the Plasmodium vivax life cycle, including hypnozoites. It is active against pre-erythrocytic (liver) and erythrocytic (asexual) forms, as well as gametocytes of P. vivax. Its activity against the pre-erythrocytic liver stages prevents the development of erythrocytic forms responsible for relapses in P. vivax malaria. Arakoda should be administered with a high-calorie, high-fat meal (~1000 calories, consisting of 19% protein, 31% carbohydrate, and 50% fat) to increase systemic absorption. Tablets should be swallowed whole and not broken, crushed, or chewed. The full course of treatment, including loading and terminal doses, should be completed. Tafenoquine should be stored at 20–25°C (68–77°F), with excursions permitted between 15–30°C (59–86°F). Both Krintafel and Arakoda should be stored in their original packaging to protect from moisture. For Krintafel, the bottle should be kept tightly closed, and the desiccant should not be removed.
